title: Chris Mason: Why Andy Burnham's about-turn on Manchester City matters
description: The rows circulating around Manchester City are huge, and they are only going to get bigger.The Premier League has concluded that City "systematically
body: The rows circulating around Manchester City are huge, and they are only going to get bigger.The Premier League has concluded that City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".This, clearly, matters for the club, but that is just the start of it. It matters for Manchester, it matters for the Premier League and so, crucially, it matters for the UK's image around the world – because England's top flight is a colossal global brand. In other words, this matters whether you like football or not.Added to all of this, Andy Burnham pitches himself as Mr Manchester and is a big football fan. The man who was the mayor of Greater Manchester a matter of months ago is now the prime minister, and so finds himself caught up in it all at a local level, a national level and a diplomatic level. Diplomatic, because rows will rage over the extent to which City's ownership is separate from the Abu Dhabi state. And the state is a big UK ally.All of this is why I thought it was in the public interest to put a series of questions to Burnham about it when I spoke to him on Wednesday as the Labour Party conference concluded in Liverpool.His comments, in his interview with me, followed by no fewer than two attempts to backtrack 24 hours later, amount to perhaps his biggest self inflicted tangle since he arrived in Downing Street in July.He will have expected to be asked about Manchester City, but he didn't expect sustained scrutiny about it.One particular exchange prompted a lot of interest. I asked if he was worried that Manchester City's owners from the United Arab Emirates might sell up.It is worth quoting his answer in full."Well, I would be really concerned to lose them. They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester. Obviously, the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is. "I can't intervene more in the process. It would be wrong for me to do that. It would be wrong, I think, to jump to a conclusion before having really studied all of the detail, but obviously it's ongoing, and because it's still contested by Manchester City, then I think it's right that I don't say much more."His answer is revealing on several levels, and was leapt on by many in football and then by the Conservatives, who labelled them "completely out of touch" and "extraordinary".Firstly, his fear – being "really concerned" – that the vast money from Abu Dhabi, that has transformed not just the club but parts of the city, could go.Secondly, that "I can't intervene more" in the process that is ongoing. What does "more" mean?To be fair, as you can see in the full quote above and he said repeatedly elsewhere in the interview, he was trying to be circumspect about it all."I am not getting directly involved in the process," he told me, later adding "I have to keep my distance from it."But, the cumulative impression many were left with was that he was sympathetic to Manchester City's situation, not least because he repeatedly compared it to a vastly smaller row involving his own club Everton's finances a few years ago."I remember people proclaiming Everton guilty at the time, and you know, with hindsight, I think more people would say that wasn't fair the way that was handled. So it would be wrong of me to leap to one side given the experience that I'd had before becoming prime minister."Everton were docked Premier League points over it.Despite the gravity and breadth of what Manchester City now confront, Andy Burnham offered no explicit criticism of them.The back pages and the sports channels as well as news sites and social media were quickly ablaze with the remarks.And by teatime on Thursday, No10 were back-pedalling.A written statement was sent out, which again is worth quoting in full:"As the prime minister made clear, the initial judgement is serious and there can't be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules. He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process. It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected."If wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences."Some 59 words that could be replaced by a picture of a reversing light – the tone and language completely different from Burnham's to me on camera.But even that statement didn't last long. Immediately, the first word of the second paragraph of it was jumped on. "If."Remember, the Premier League says Manchester City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of almost a billion pounds. The club deny wrongdoing and are considering an appeal, but the Premier League's conclusion is clear.But Downing Street said "if." Fast forward a little over an hour, and the statement was re-issued. "If" became "wherever."In real time, No10's jitters and discomfort about this was there for all to see.The prime minister seen as Mr Manchester, who loves his football and revels in a man of the people image, caught up in one of the biggest domestic stories of the year and one that is only just beginning.It is won't be the last time he faces questions about Manchester City.

schema.headline: Chris Mason: Why Andy Burnham's about-turn on Manchester City matters

title: Lawyer for Cornell accuser says university doctor was 'yet another failure'
description: A woman who has accused several men of raping her at Cornell University in 2024 was failed by the school's health system, her lawyer has said.Jane Doe
body: A woman who has accused several men of raping her at Cornell University in 2024 was failed by the school's health system, her lawyer has said.Jane Doe, as she is known in court filings, said she told a university doctor two days after the alleged assault that she had contracted a urinary tract infection "in a traumatic way", but that they "didn't really follow up", according to the New York Times, external.Her lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, said in a statement provided to the BBC that the doctor visit marked "yet another failure by Cornell".Cornell said it did not have any additional information to share in response to an inquiry from the BBC about the health visit.After Doe was seen by the university doctor, she said she was then told to go to therapy, documents from the institution's investigation show."Ms Doe's disclosure warranted further inquiry, including a rape kit and consultation of medical professionals trained to deal with rape cases and a physical exam to document her injuries," Giuffra said in a statement to the BBC."Inexplicably, all the medical professional did was to advise Ms Doe to 'speak with somebody'."  The woman filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university in September, alleging she was drugged and raped by seven men at a fraternity house at the university in 2024. She also alleged that Cornell failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved. The case was referred to Tompkins County District Attorney's Office, the top prosecutor in the county, back in 2024.District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said his office did not bring charges at the time because he had only seen a statement from Doe implying the incident was consensual and that she had not been drugged. This week, Van Houten's office announced it would be reopening the case - less than two weeks after Doe filed her civil lawsuit.Cornell has said it provided evidence to the district attorney's office from its own investigation, including a Snapchat group chat in which fraternity members discussed a "free" sexual encounter with Doe on the night of the alleged assault. Giuffra accused the district attorney of changing "his story so many times, I can't keep up with it" in his latest statement. "The pattern I am seeing is that whenever evidence comes out supporting prosecution, he claims he never saw it," Giuffra said. "His defensiveness and attempt to save face has not been impressive."Van Houten told the BBC that he had received a six-page statement from Jane Doe and the Snapchat messages from campus police. But there was also a 120-page transcript from a recording of an interview by a Title IX investigator with Doe, with a victim's advocate, a counsellor and one of Doe's attorneys participating by phone, which Van Houten said he had not seen in full at the time."The full transcript – which I have now obtained – confirms the contents of Jane Doe's sworn statement," he said. "I have no intention of letting Mr Giuffra's unfair criticism distract my office from getting to the truth."The documents from the university's Title IX review provide the most detailed account yet into the three weeks after Doe was allegedly assaulted and made the decision to report to the university. Title IX is a federal civil rights law mandating that universities follow certain rules when investigating sexual assaults.The morning after the alleged assault, when Doe returned to her sorority house, she told her two roommates she had done drugs and had sex with multiple men, but did not yet use the word "rape" or "assault", according to the roommates. She appeared to be "in shock" and "not really understanding the gravity of what she was saying", a roommate said, according to the documents the New York Times obtained. The review also included Doe's text exchanges with one of the men accused of assault, who apologised to her after the alleged rape. "I just wanted to apologize for how things went down the other night," he wrote. He said he and other men accused of assault felt awful for being too intoxicated to "shut it down and kick people out before it got way out of hand". Her roommate told the university that as time went on, Doe "kind of came to realise that it was something bad. And that she didn't really enjoy her time there".On 3 November, Doe texted one of the men accused of assault and told him, "let's be clear that 90% of what happened that night was not consensual. i was given more key than i can remember," she said, using a shorthand for ketamine. "I know that i told u i felt uncomfortable and i didn't know anyone in the room," the text messages included in the document read. Later, at the Title IX interview, she said she felt "100 percent" confident that she was raped, remarks her attorney confirmed to the BBC. Doe went to get a rape kit on 7 November, three weeks after the alleged assault took place, but no DNA evidence was recovered, her lawyer said.Giuffra said that if she had received a rape kit in October when she went to see the university doctor, it is likely there would have been DNA evidence. The lawyer said the messages and other interviews from the investigation show that "Ms Doe's internal processing went from denial, to shame and ultimately acceptance that she had been raped by people that she thought were her friends". "Her reactions were a textbook reaction to trauma," he added. At the sprawling university tucked away in upstate New York, the tension on campus is palpable. The BBC spoke to students and a faculty member at Cornell, all of whom asked to remain anonymous. Many others were reluctant and very uncomfortable to speak about the incident.One female student, who is now a senior and was on campus in 2024, recalled how hard it was living there at the time, particularly as rumours began spreading about Doe.Now, two years later, she told the BBC how she and her friends felt "overwhelmed" and "disappointed", comparing the atmosphere on campus to a "dark cloud". Cornell, she believes, mishandled the situation.A faculty member also called the mood "dismal". Staff were not trained therapists so it was hard to know how to navigate a moment like this, she said, and many of her colleagues felt at a loss for words."I just don't understand."If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide., externalA list of UK organisations that can help is available here.

schema.headline: Lawyer for Cornell accuser says university doctor was 'yet another failure'

title: What's really going on in lymphatic drainage beauty trend videos?
description: Image source, Abbey AlexandraImage caption, Abbey Alexandra performs lymphatic drainage massages a couple of times a weekByEmily HoltIf she's ever fee
body: Image source, Abbey AlexandraImage caption, Abbey Alexandra performs lymphatic drainage massages a couple of times a weekByEmily HoltIf she's ever feeling bloated, Abbey Alexandra has a go-to routine, using body oil and a wooden roller to perform stomach massages.She shares before-and-after videos on TikTok, saying she feels the process leaves her depuffed and defined: "You definitely feel a lot better after, they are relaxing."The technique is a form of lymphatic drainage massage, adapted from a medical treatment and shared as a beauty trend. Celebrity fans include Maya Jama, who shares her clinic sessions, and actress Hailey Bieber, who told Time magazine: "I swear by them."Whether there is a physical change - or any need for one - is debatable, but fans of the massages claim they help "flatten" and "debloat" and give a "snatched waist" and "sculpted abs". But what's actually happening to their bodies?What do the videos show?Image source, Abbey AlexandraImage caption, Before-and-after video grabs of a form of lymphatic drainage massage Many videos on social media promoting lymphatic massage show a woman either standing sideways, facing the front or perhaps lying down with her stomach showing a slight - and very normal - curve outwards.Then begins the methodical massage in circular motions seemingly draining fluid away. By the end, her stomach appears flatter - if a little red.But social media body trends should always be viewed with scepticism, says Dr Ella Guest, senior research fellow and health psychologist at the Centre for Appearance Research based at the University of the West of England."These images might be altered using photo-editing tools or filters, people standing in particular poses, use of lighting, lots could even be AI-generated," she says."I think stopping to reflect on what you see and questioning whether it looks realistic, or if it's very aligned with beauty standards, can be useful. Remember, if something looks too good to be true, it probably is."What is the lymphatic system? The lymphatic system is a network of channels and glands throughout the body that helps fight infection and remove excess fluid, according to the NHS.Dr Xand van Tulleken tells Morning Live that the lymphatic system helps remove excess fluid from tissues and supports the immune system."When it is not working properly, it can contribute to swelling, which can be a condition called lymphoedema."This commonly affects people who have cancers that involve the lymph system or who've had treatment involving the lymph nodes.It causes swelling in any part of the body, but usually develops in the arms or legs."In simple terms, the lymphatic system helps keep your body's fluid levels balanced, cleans up waste, and supports your defences against illness," says van Tulleken.Draining your lymphatic systemDr Xand explains how to drain your lymphatic system.What's the massage doing?Image source, Abbey AlexandraImage caption, Abbey says lymphatic drainage massage makes her feel less bloatedDr Xand says manual lymphatic drainage is one of a range of treatments used by medical professionals "if your lymphatic system isn't working as it should". He describes it as using "light pressure" and "strategic massage techniques" to "clear" your lymphatic system. "They'll coax excess lymph fluid from your swollen tissues toward your lymph nodes, where the lymph can reabsorb," he says - adding lymph nodes are found in the armpits, neck and groin. He adds that these massages can be a "safe way" to relieve symptoms for conditions like lymphoedema but are not suitable for some people with pre-existing medical conditions. He stresses: "No one should get their health advice from Instagram - far safer to use the NHS website, or consult your GP."Abbey, who has endometriosis which she says causes her to feel bloated, began doing her own massage routines twice a week aer seeing social media posts about lymphatic drainage."I started using my hands and then I bought some wooden tools as well."After doing my routine, I personally feel less puffy and bloated, particularly around my stomach."Visually, I notice that my stomach looks a little more defined and I also feel lighter and more comfortable."Does it work?Figure caption, Draining your lymphatic systemDr Xand says there is "no need" for most people to perform lymphatic drainage treatments at home."There is very little high-quality evidence showing they provide meaningful or lasting benefits for healthy individuals, and it does not promote fat loss," he says.But he does note that lymphatic drainage massages can feel "relaxing" and some people "can notice a temporary reduction in swelling"."For most healthy people, regular movement, exercise and staying hydrated are all that's needed to support normal lymphatic function," he says."Unless someone has a diagnosed lymphatic condition, I don't think anyone needs routine lymphatic drainage treatments, despite the growing popularity of these practices on social media."For Abbey, it's something she enjoys. "I know the visual difference is temporary... But I do like how I look and feel afterwards so it'll always be a part of my routine."However, Guest warns striving for a sculpted stomach could "feed into people's insecurities"."We know that when we compare ourselves online and try to live up to these trends, we tend to scrutinise our appearance more and feel less satisfied with how we look," she says."The reality is that healthy bodies come in a wide range of shapes and sizes."

schema.headline: What's really going on in lymphatic drainage beauty trend videos?

title: What's gone wrong at Nike? How the world's sportswear giant lost its mojo
description: It's been a difficult few years for Nike.The largest sportswear brand on the planet, named after the ancient Greek goddess of victory, has been losing
body: It's been a difficult few years for Nike.The largest sportswear brand on the planet, named after the ancient Greek goddess of victory, has been losing of late. Losing sales, losing customers and losing ground to its rivals.The one-time industry disruptor is now the establishment and in the middle of a tricky turnaround plan aimed at clinging on to market dominance.Nike's latest financial results show signs a turnaround strategy put in place by company veteran Elliott Hill, who was coaxed out of retirement two years ago to lead the firm, is working - but the pace of change is more marathon than sprint.However, its recovery has been dented by the loss of football star Kylian Mbappé, who ended his 20-year association with the brand last week to join fast-growing Swiss rival, On.The Real Madrid striker's departure raises the question of whether Nike can remain the top logo for not just elite athletes, but also the fans that idolise them.To be clear, Nike is still a mega brand and popular the world over. But missteps have seen hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off its stock market value as its share price tumbled by 75% over five years. Last month, Nike was ejected from the S&P 100 stock market index of the biggest blue-chip firms in the US.So what's gone wrong? And can Hill turn things around?Matt Powell, a veteran analyst and adviser in the sports retail industry, reckons Nike has made "several strategic errors" which have been difficult to reverse, including cutting ties with retailers to sell only direct to customers online and making limited editions items more available."The more broadly available those shoes became, the fewer people were interested," Powell says.Other self-inflicted wounds he suggests include spending research and development cash on digital operations rather than new products."They really shut down their innovation on product. Someone jokingly said they were trying to turn Nike into eBay."The gamble - spending its entire basketball budget on Jordan before he had even competed in the NBA - made Nike what it is today. The company built a shoe brand around him - Air Jordan. The red and black colours broke NBA rules, but Nike used it as a marketing stunt and paid the fines.In years that followed Nike partnered with generational talents Tiger Woods, Serena Williams and Cristiano Ronaldo, who all donned the Swoosh on their way to golf, tennis and football greatness.While the brand retains partnerships with long-retired Jordan, plus Williams and Ronaldo - Woods ended his association in 2024."[I'm] not saying that what they did wasn't great, but it was in the past," said Tim Derdenger, an academic in marketing and strategy. "It's not the future and it's not the current and that is what drives apparel sales today."Nike's books still boast top athletes, ranging from Rory McIlory to Vinicius Junior.  However, it has now lost its biggest footballing star in Mbappé, who had been with Nike since he was nine years old, along with World Cup winner Lamine Yamal.Yamal suggested his move to Adidas gave him the chance to stand out from Nike's star-studded roster, while Mbappé said On would see him "surrounded by innovators who dream of the same things I do".Was that a parting dig at Nike? For all the "doom and gloom", Nike will stay number one, according to Powell - millions worldwide, including young people, remain loyal - but its mistakes have dented its dominance. "Will Nike be the gorilla they once were? I don't think so. Can the brand come back to growth and profitability? Yes," Powell says."When you shut down innovation, you don't turn it back on and it goes right back to full speed," he adds.Powell thinks Nike's turnaround plan, called "Sport Offense", will start to show positive signs next year.Hill said Nike had "more work to do" on its sportswear, Jordan brand and in China as the company announced quarterly revenues of $11bn (£8.3bn), which undershot analysts' expectations.Notably, the company cited "headwinds" in China, where revenue declined by 26%.

schema.headline: What's gone wrong at Nike? How the world's sportswear giant lost its mojo

title: US says Europe should ready fuel supplies as Trump threatens diesel ban
description: Donald Trump has said he may ask European countries to release some of their diesel reserves as he mulls a ban on US exports of the fuel amid a global
body: Donald Trump has said he may ask European countries to release some of their diesel reserves as he mulls a ban on US exports of the fuel amid a global shortage.The comments followed his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urging for Europe to immediately ready and release such supplies. "American farmers, truckers, and businesses should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar, he argued.The US has threatened to restrict diesel exports amid surging costs due to the war in Iran. The issue is top of mind for US voters ahead of the crucial midterm elections. On Thursday, Britain held talks with European partners about the potential release of diesel reserves in response to any ban.The US is a vital supplier of diesel to the world, exporting between 1.2 and 1.5 million barrels per day, with experts warning a ban on shipments abroad could put further pressure on prices in other countries."We're thinking about it very seriously," Trump said of an export ban at the weekend.On Thursday Trump added that he may ask European countries to release some of their diesel reserves, while Bessent said they should do so "immediately"."Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions," Bessent said in a post on social media.The plans come weeks ahead of November elections in the US, where control of Congress will be up for grabs. The president is set to travel across the US campaigning for Republicans in hopes of keeping control of the House and Senate.Diesel prices in the UK hit record highs this week and are hovering just under 200p per litre, according to motoring organisation the RAC.Britain's Energy Minister Martin McCluskey was on a call with European counterparts on Thursday to discuss the potential ban.A source familiar with the discussions told the BBC it was prudent to prepare a co-ordinated response with other countries, including those across EU, but added that there were still European reserves left from a coordinated release of strategic fuel stocks earlier in the year."We have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry," a government spokesperson said. The government has stressed that there is no cause for concern about potential diesel shortages, though prices are expected to rise further.A European Commission spokesperson said today that there were "lots of calls, lots of meetings" taking place on the diesel situation, including with "high level contacts" in the US administration.Prices of petrol and diesel globally have skyrocketed since the outbreak of the US-Israel war in Iran in February. The closure of the vital Strait of Hormuz, which typically transports around a fifth of the world's oil and gas, has pushed up the price of products made from oil.An export ban from Russia, also a major supplier of diesel, has added to the pressure on prices.Trump has argued that keeping any surplus barrels of diesel in the US would lower pump prices domestically, offering immediate relief to drivers, truckers, and businesses ahead of the midterm elections.But David Fyfe, chief economist at Argus Media, said cutting off American supply would likely cause international prices to skyrocket.Diesel prices have hit an all-time high in the UK, with the latest RAC figures showing average pump prices at 199.79p per litre, up from 142.38pDiesel is harder to refine than gasoline and, because it is used by the haulage industry and in agriculture, it is very difficult to reduce demand.The UK is heavily reliant on imports. Although the four refineries in the UK make more than enough petrol to meet demand, they do not make enough diesel for the country's needs.There were 15.1 million diesel vehicles on UK roads at the end of June, according to the Department for Transport. That is a drop from 15.7 million a year before.There were 9.8 million diesel cars, down year on year from 10.4 million.

schema.headline: US says Europe should ready fuel supplies as Trump threatens diesel ban

title: Christa Pike in critical condition after surviving two lethal injections, lawyer says
description: Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike is in "critical condition, receiving life-saving care" at hospital, after surviving two lethal injection attem
body: Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike is in "critical condition, receiving life-saving care" at hospital, after surviving two lethal injection attempts, leading the state's governor to halt all executions for the year."We don't have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment," her lawyer Randy Spivey told reporters on Thursday. "But we do know that she is alive right now." Her lawyers are now asking for her sentence to be commuted. Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer. She was injected with two lethal doses of pentobarbital on Wednesday but remained alive, her lawyers said. She was then sent to hospital in an ambulance.Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer.Her attempted execution on Wednesday was the subject of a last-minute legal battle. This culminated in the US Supreme Court allowing the lethal injections to go ahead.Slemmer's mother May Martinez, who was among those who wanted the execution to take place and who travelled to Tennessee to witness it, told NBC News after the botched attempt that "it was a mess".On Thursday afternoon, Pike's lawyers offered more details about what happened during the attempted execution, describing a harrowing scene shrouded in secrecy. "Last night, the execution team attempted to establish an IV line for an hour," Spivey said. "I counted at least seven needles used in her left arm alone, one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her arm after an unsuccessful attempt."Spivey said that observers were kept in a dark room behind a closed curtain, after the second lethal dose had been administered and "it was clear that Miss Pike was still breathing" minutes later."No-one knew what was going on behind that curtain," Spivey said. "I had no idea when and if medical professionals began to assist."Spivey said the state's governor must commute Christa's sentence now,  a request that was denied previously.Stephen Ferrell, another of Pike's lawyers, said they were also looking at other legal options.  "We want to think this through and we want to make sure that Christa recovers and has some input in what she wants," he said.Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered an independent review and said on Thursday the investigation into Pike's botched execution "will be thorough", adding that "it's going to take time"."There are a lot of questions," Lee said. "The people of our state deserve to have those questions answered, and that's what this investigation is for." Lee has not made clear who will conduct the independent review of the state's execution procedures. His order to pause all executions will overlap with the planned 3 December execution of convicted murderer Gary Sutton.The Tennessee Department of Correction, which handled the execution, issued a statement defending its handling of the case. It said in a statement that it "followed every step of the State's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the attorney general's office"."The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening."Pike was given two doses of the chemical pentobarbital, in accordance with state protocol when the first attempt fails, but was still alive afterwards, according to court filings by her lawyers."This execution is causing Ms Pike unnecessary agony and occurring in violation of his right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment," her lawyers said.The Tennessee attorney general's office said in a statement that it agreed with the decision to call for an investigation, adding: "We need to know what happened."US Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn, who is running for Tennessee governor, described the situation as "tragic"."While there should be a thorough review of what happened and why the process failed, the answer is simple: bring back the electric chair," Blackburn said.Democrat Jerri Green, Blackburn's opponent, criticised her for wanting to "bring back one of the most cruel forms of capital punishment". "As governor, I would put a moratorium on all future executions," Green said on X.This is the second time in 2026 Tennessee officials attempted and failed to execute a prisoner. In May, the execution of Tony Carruthers was called off after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal drug. Carruthers was given a year's reprieve.With additional reporting by Stephanie Hegarty, World Service correspondent

schema.headline: Christa Pike in critical condition after surviving two lethal injections, lawyer says

title: Coroner warns of risk of future deaths at mental health unit where patient was killed
description: On the night of Cahan's death, staff on the ward were found to have been asleep on the job and on their phones for long periods.  East London NHS Foun
body: On the night of Cahan's death, staff on the ward were found to have been asleep on the job and on their phones for long periods.  East London NHS Foundation Trust (ELFT) says the failings identified were "wholly unacceptable" and that it has undertaken a "significant programme of work" to improve inpatient services.The coroner's Prevention of Future Deaths report highlights 14 concerns. These include failing to carry out "timely and thorough observations" of patients, then falsifying records "in the safe knowledge that staff on duty would not report or escalate the deception". The document also says there were delays in starting CPR on Cahan when he was discovered, that staff misled the police as to what the patients had been doing on the night of the incident, and that staff colluded with each other to take two-hour unauthorised breaks.Torres-Pena was given a hospital order with no time limit after pleading guilty to manslaughter by diminished responsibility in 2023.The coroner also raised concerns that many of the failings had been brought up at a previous inquest he'd conducted."The findings in this inquest are strikingly similar to the findings of an inquest before this court in 2021, remedial measures reported in that case do not appear to have been implemented effectively by the trust", the report says."Findings of dishonesty on this scale are extraordinarily rare in a coronial investigation. The public are entitled to expect a clear explanation of how this was allowed to happen and what is being done to ensure it never happens again," says James Cahan, the family solicitor and Hugo's cousin.

schema.headline: Coroner warns of risk of future deaths at mental health unit where patient was killed

title: Putin warns West that Russia is ready to use every weapon to protect Kaliningrad
description: Vladimir Putin has said Russia will use all weapons at his disposal if it considers its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad to have come under direct attack
body: Vladimir Putin has said Russia will use all weapons at his disposal if it considers its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad to have come under direct attack.The Russian president insisted that Moscow was "not threatening anyone" and merely responding to statements by Western leaders that it was preparing for war in 2029 or 2030.Throughout this week, Russia has accused Nato of preparing to blockade its territory, which borders Lithuania and Poland, warning that it would even be prepared to use nuclear weapons if the West tried to cut off Kaliningrad from the rest of Russia.Nato has sought to calm the situation, stressing that it was a defensive alliance and urging Moscow to stop its "nuclear threats".Western allies have faced a surge in so-called hybrid warfare incidents blamed on Russia, particularly in Poland and the Baltics in recent months. Last week alone, Poland said a Russian helicopter had strayed into its territory adjacent to Kaliningrad and Lithuania said its population felt "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace.German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Thursday that his country was preparing for further hybrid attacks, "including serious ones", after a drone armed with explosives was found in August on the tarmac at Leipzig airport close to Ukrainian cargo planes.In a wide-ranging speech at the Valdai foreign policy forum, Putin told his audience that he believed that international conflicts were highly likely to continue, but would get better as "Western hegemony" weakened.Although the Russian leader himself began the full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022, he again blamed the West for provoking the invasion, arguing that Moscow had simply been forced to defend itself and take up arms.He also insisted that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian economic targets were a direct response to Ukraine's strikes on Russia's oil refineries and its ships in the Black Sea."Now from every direction we're receiving calls 'let's stop'. But they started it," he said.Putin admitted Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP. Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helped the Kremlin finance the war.Russia has targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since the war in Ukraine started in 2022. Other civilian infrastructure is also regularly hit, with a key bridge in Kyiv attacked by drones on Thursday.Putin also accused the West of instigating other conflicts."If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation, in this case we are talking about Kaliningrad but possibly some other territories, of course the issue of use by the Russian Federation of all arms at the disposal of our country will inevitably and immediately be on the agenda," he said.He accused Nato of holding naval manoeuvres in the Baltic Sea that he argued represented serious threats to Kaliningrad. If the territory came under Western blockade, he said Russia would be prepared to use all means and forces, including nuclear."We are not threatening anyone. We do not intend to attack anyone in 2029, in 2030, in 2050. But if we come across an aggression we will have to respond. Citizens of European countries should be fully aware of that."He added that while he was aware of the nuclear capabilities of countries such as the UK and France, the weapons at its disposal were unparalleled. Western officials have long feared that, rather than invading Kaliningrad, Russia would use the relatively small distance between the exclave and ally Belarus - known as the Suwalki Gap - were it to attempt to seize Lithuanian territory by force.Lithuania's prime minister told the BBC last week that his country had made evacuation plans in case Russia invaded and thousands of Nato troops are stationed there.Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte made clear on Wednesday that none of the alliance's "exercises or activities" posed any threat to Moscow and that the Kremlin's messaging was "absolutely not called for and not helpful".Putin spent some time talking about leading countries in the world having armaments at their disposal that could "swipe away all life or at least push the Earth to catastrophic consequences", and said that unfortunately no-one could be sure they would never be used.He drew the analogy of a gun sitting on a theatre stage - if it was hanging there at the start of the show, it would certainly be fired at the end.He appeared to call for the rules of warfare to be rewritten and warned of the increasing risk of artificial intelligence."The automation and digitalisation of warfare leads to its gamification. This leads to degradation and sliding back of humanity to barbarity," he said.

schema.headline: Putin warns West that Russia is ready to use every weapon to protect Kaliningrad

title: Flydubai attacker 'underwent Islamist radical indoctrination', Netanyahu says
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesByOlivia IrelandIsraeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says investigations suggest the man who stabbed his fellow
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesByOlivia IrelandIsraeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says investigations suggest the man who stabbed his fellow pilot and tried to take over a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".The Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two hours into its journey on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control to land safely.Netanyahu told Fox News that it was looking "very likely" that the attacker, who he said was an Omani national, "was going to down the plane".Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) state news agency reports investigations have begun there to determine "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose".The Interior Ministry of Saudi Arabia - where the plane made an emergency landing - said that both the pilot and co-pilot had been sent back to the UAE on Thursday morning after medical teams had cleared them.UAE officials earlier claimed jurisdiction over the incident because the aircraft on which the attack took place is registered there and flies under its flag.Netanyahu told Fox that once the attacker had been subdued and tied up by passengers and crew, he was "calling out to the aircrew 'kill me, kill me', so it's clear he was suicidal - that's not a question".Figure caption, Passenger Almog Itali said it felt like a "rollercoaster" as Flight FZ1073 fell 17,000ft in less than two minutes"And with all the passengers in there, and if you couple that with what I just told you about the Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that were found in his background, I think... that'll give us a pretty good clue."However, he stressed that he did not want to draw any firm conclusions as to motive yet.Both US President Donald Trump and UAE officials have indicated to the media that Iran may be responsible for the incident, without definitively blaming Tehran.Trump told reporters on Thursday that Iran would be "hit very hard" if it was deemed to have been involved in the attack.Pilots from countries without diplomatic relations with Israel were usually not allowed to fly there, Netanyahu said when asked about how the suspected Omani pilot came to be on the plane.He added: "Obviously there was a loophole here and we're taking care of that among other things... with the full co-operation, I have to say, of the Emirati government, so we're both interested in making sure this doesn't happen again." Oman has not formally established official ties with Israel, unlike the UAE.The prime minister was also asked earlier on the same network whether there was an indication if Iran was involved, he replied: "It's too early to say".Both Netanyahu and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the stabbed pilot, Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar was a "hero". India's ambassador to the UAE Deepak Mittal visited Captain Machhar in hospital on Thursday, the Indian Mission confirmed on social media, stating he was "in good health and recovering well". Image source, Embassy of India in IsraelImage caption, The Indian government has praised Smit Machchhar for his "immense courage"Preliminary findings from a separate Israeli investigation into the incident, suggest that the alleged attacker intended to crash the plane, an Israeli security source told BBC Arabic.The source said the investigation - led by Israel's intelligence agency Mossad - interviewed passengers after they arrived in Tel Aviv to establish what had happened on the plane.Flydubai's flight FZ1073, with more than 170 people on board, took off from Dubai International Airport in the UAE at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time), en route to Ben Gurion Airport.Two hours later, the 17,000ft drop in altitude was reported on the plane tracking website Flightradar24 and minutes later the plane signalled an emergency code.At about 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent, landing safely at  Tabuk Airport in the north west of Saudi.Flydubai has since suspended flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv as it carried out its own investigation into the incident.Israel's Transportation Ministry said the suspension aligns with Netanyahu's directive.Israeli airlines including El Al, Israir and Arkia said plans were in place to operate rescue flights from Dubai starting on Friday to bring back stranded passengers. The Transportation Ministry also said it sent an urgent request to Etihad Airlines to increase the number of flights between Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv.

schema.headline: Flydubai attacker 'underwent Islamist radical indoctrination', Netanyahu says

title: Crypto thieves attacked man in home and threatened to kill pregnant wife's baby in 'horrific' robbery
description: Warning: This story contains distressing detailsA businessman was beaten with hammers by masked men who broke into his home and threatened to kill his
body: Warning: This story contains distressing detailsA businessman was beaten with hammers by masked men who broke into his home and threatened to kill his heavily pregnant wife unless he transferred hundreds of thousands of pounds of cryptocurrency.Speaking to the BBC, the couple, who want to remain anonymous, described the attack as "horrific" and said they feared for their unborn baby's life.The attackers left in a car driven by a getaway driver after the man transferred his crypto savings. Crimestoppers are offering a £10,000 reward for information in the attack, which was captured on home security footage and is being investigated by the police.Experts say it is one of a growing type of violent theft known as a "wrench attack" targeting cryptocurrency investors. As crypto coins have risen in value, reports of these violent robberies linked to digital assets have emerged in the UK, France and the US.Once funds are transferred, recovering them can be extremely difficult.The man, who the BBC is calling James, said three intruders forced their way into their Solihull home before launching an assault which lasted 45 minutes."The door gets pushed open, I can see gloves coming in, balaclavas," he said.James tried to fight the men off but they hit him in the face, head and ribs with hammers.His wife, who was seven months pregnant, was held down on the sofa by one of the criminals. "He's got a pillow over her face," James said. "He's literally suffocating her on the sofa. I can hear her screaming, 'I can't breathe'."The couple still had no idea what the criminals wanted until one of the men demanded James unlock his phone and hand it over.James said the attackers appeared to know he owned cryptocurrency, but had little understanding of how to access it.Instead, they were taking instructions from someone else connected via a live video call."I can hear the guy on FaceTime saying: 'Show me everything on his phone. Show me what apps he's got'," he said.When the caller identified a crypto wallet containing substantial funds, the threats escalated dramatically."He was basically saying: 'Look, if you don't send us this money now, we're going to stab your wife in the stomach and kill your baby. We're going to kill your wife'," James said.His wife, who also did not want to be named, described the attack that happened in December last year as "horrific" and said she feared James had been killed when he was unresponsive on the floor."It was terrifying," she said.The woman, in her early thirties, was expecting her third child at the time and said she feared she might lose the baby due to the stress of the attack. The baby survived and was born at full term. The men left after James transferred his savings - hundreds of thousands of pounds of cryptocurrency - to the digital wallet of the man on the video call.They also stole several luxury Rolex watches.James said before they left, he heard the man on the video call tell his accomplices: "You can have 10 grand each but I am taking the rest."Unlike money held in a conventional bank account, cryptocurrency is often controlled directly by the owner through digital wallets or physical storage devices. For criminals, that combination of speed, anonymity and irreversibility can make crypto holders attractive targets.Whilst the vast majority of cryptocurrency theft happens online through hacks and scams, crypto investigators at Chainalysis say "wrench attacks" have surged in recent years.According to their research, $30m (£22.6m) had been stolen so far this year up to June in violent robberies, making 2026 likely to become the single-worst year for violent crypto attacks on record. Home invasions are also on the rise this year, it found.The US, Brazil, and Thailand are hotspots but France has seen the largest number of attacks by far, as a result of a data breach at a tax office that has apparently allowed wealthy crypto holders to be located."The physical security assumptions that protect traditional wealth, such as bank vaults and armored cars, do not automatically apply in crypto. Often, holders keep their assets in comparatively low security setups, like self-custody wallets, that can be compromised without any institutional gatekeeper standing in the way," said researchers in their report.James said he became an amateur investor in crypto coins in 2020 and made enough money to quit his job in 2023 to trade full time.Now he has lost everything and is looking to get back to his traditional job.Police have yet to identify the attackers.Crimestoppers is offering a £10,000 reward for information leading to progress in the investigation.Alan Edwards from the charity hopes people might have information about the three attackers, the driver who was parked outside without a face covering, or the man on the phone."These criminals are obviously serious and part of some kind of organised crime gang," he said."People might be scared to give us information but we are independent of the police and keep people completely anonymous."The three attackers are all thought to be in their late teens or early 20s and one of them was a black male with a scar under his left eyebrow.James said he has little hope of recovering the stolen funds, but instead wanted to see those responsible brought to justice.He also wants his experience to serve as a warning."They threatened my wife and my baby," he said. "People need to understand these risks are real."

schema.headline: Crypto thieves attacked man in home and threatened to kill pregnant wife's baby in 'horrific' robbery

title: Celebrity Traitors: Chaos, coffins and ‘Claudiapatra’ steal the show
description: Figure caption, Watch: Celebrity Traitors series two kicks off with a wild curveballByHelen BushbyCulture reporter Spoiler warning: This article revea
body: Figure caption, Watch: Celebrity Traitors series two kicks off with a wild curveballByHelen BushbyCulture reporter Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the first episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.One person in particular may have dominated much of this opening episode, but Claudia Winkleman's gothic arrival still caused a stir.Carried aloft by druids in a closed coffin, the show's host arrived in a church, to greet 21 anxious-looking celebrities."That was quite the nap," she said as she emerged."Claudiapatra!" gasped model and actress Jerry Hall - spotting similarities in both grandeur and hairstyles between Claudia and Cleopatra, the Egyptian queen.Winkleman said at the show's press launch she loved her "iconic entrance",  but admitted she'd initially wanted to hide in the castle's suit of armour."It's like a sort of GCSE history fantasy - it was either that or the grandfather clock," she said.Image source, BBC/Studio LambertImage caption, Claudia Winkleman emerged from her coffin to greet the celebrities in churchImage caption, Jerry Hall referenced Cleopatra, seen here played by the late actress and former MP Glenda Jackson in a 1971 BBC Morecambe and Wise sketch But the main talking point of this show was actor Richard E Grant, with his shocking admission.Grant and presenter Maya Jama were selected as two of Winkleman's three traitors.But immediately afterwards, Grant appeared to forget the entire point of the game, by gleefully blurting out to those around him he was actually a traitor.You could have heard a pin drop after he said it. Stunned silence."It's an interesting angle," laughed singer James Blunt just afterwards, while comic Rob Beckett told him: "I think you've just done something that's never happened in the game - it is a bold strategy."Grant later admitted, in footage for viewers of the show: "That may be the biggest mistake I have ever made in my life. I was so thrilled to have been chosen as a traitor that in my unguarded excitement, I said, 'Of course I'm a traitor'."I clearly need to defuse all the heat that's coming in my direction."Image source, BBC/Studio LambertImage caption, Can Richard E Grant hold his nerve in this episode?Ex-BBC journalist Amol Rajan swooped the following day, asking Grant: "What happened last night?"But instead of sowing clever seeds of doubt, Grant said he'd been so "blatant" about wanting to be a traitor that he simply responded he was one, when he was asked.It was an odd reply, perhaps because he was flustered.Rajan labelled him the "Lord of Chaos", but Hall stayed loyal."I just don't believe Richard's a traitor, I've known him 30 years and he's my neighbour," she said."He says and does eccentric things, he's an amazing guy, but I think he's acting out because he's not been chosen."Hall's loyalty could be tested though, given Alan Carr murdered Paloma Faith in series one by touching her face.Comic and writer Miranda Hart also thinks Grant could be a faithful, but admitted she is confused. Winkleman told the press launch she thought Grant blurted out his identity in error, because he was so thrilled to be a traitor."He was giddy, wasn't he? He's just laughing at what's happening. Fantastic," she said.Ed Gamble, the host of BBC One and BBC Sounds spin-off show Uncloaked, added: "It felt like he'd been given the lead role in a film and he just had to tell everyone. It's such an insane moment."Grant may find that no one tells him a secret ever again.He did eventually decide to let the much more cool, calm and collected Jama take the lead in their subsequent decision making.Image source, BBC/Studio LambertImage caption, Ross Kemp took joint charge of the mission along with James BluntMeanwhile the other celebrities also proved their worth on the show, not least "hard man" Ross Kemp, the former EastEnders actor-turned documentary-maker, whose programmes have focused on gangs and the armed forces.Having admitted how nervous he was in the pews of the church, he came into his own for the task, along with ex-army captain James Blunt.They divided the celebrities into teams, leading them to successfully find the treasure on the pirate ship, bagging £15,000.But Kemp quickly crumbled back in the castle, when paranoia set in.The Last of Us and Game of Thrones star Bella Ramsey, a key player in the task, had grabbed a captain's hat from the boat. She playfully planted it on Kemp's head, marking their victory.Little Mix's Leigh-Anne Pinnock then touched Kemp on the arm as she walked through the bar.Clearly remembering how Carr killed off Faith early on, Kemp got understandably fearful he had been killed by a traitor.This tickled Gamble, who said: "It is one of the funniest things I've ever seen - the moment he gets touched on the arm, having already thought Bella Ramsey putting a captain's hat on him is a murder in plain sight."What a variety of men live within the Ross Kemp sphere."He's a big hard man running that mission. And then immediately terrified of a member of Little Mix touching him on the arm. That's incredible."Image source, BBC/Studio LambertImage caption, Actress Myha'la added she wants to be perceived as "doughy-eyed, fun, and maybe a little naïve", unlike her character in IndustryWe also learned that although quite a few celebrities wanted to be traitors, including Rajan and Beckett, comics James Acaster and Hart and mathematician Hannah Fry wanted to be faithfuls - Fry said she was "dripping with prefect energy".Meanwhile YouTuber King Kenny and actress Myha'la had their own strategies."I have an innocent face; I want to avenge Niko [Omilana, the first to be banished in series one]. He left too early," Kenny said, while  Myha'la added she wants to be perceived as "doughy-eyed, fun, and maybe a little naïve", unlike her scheming character in Industry.Fashion is likely to be another talking point in the castle.Beckett observed that when actress Julie Hesmondhalgh wore the shield she'd won, she looked like a "cardinal" in her long, red dress, adding:  "I thought we were in the Vatican!"True to form, Joe Lycett wore a polka-dot shorts suit with a purple feather collar.Hall was also keen to strut her stuff, saying she wanted to stay long enough to "wear all my fabulous outfits".Blunt deadpanned: "Well, look, if you go early, I'll wear your outfits."But although the one-liners were flying, the show got very serious at the end, when the game's new twist dictated that Grant and Jama had to select their third traitor.They had to choose two celebrities to meet them in person, to argue why they should stay, with the winner joining them and the loser becoming the show's first murder victim."They'll beg – there is a God. I'm loving it. Delicious," Grant said, grinning like a kid in a sweet shop.Image source, BBC/Studio LambertImage caption, Last man standing? Amol Rajan and James Acaster battle for survival in the churchRajan and Acaster were chosen, having both put pressure on Grant over being a traitor."Amol is the biggest Rottweiler on me; it would take the heat off me for having been such a plonker," he admitted, while adding: "James Acaster is laser-eyed in his conviction that I am a traitor."Despite wanting to be a faithful, Acaster argued a solid case to stay, telling Grant: "If I go tonight, the first person they're looking at is you."Rajan then took the floor, saying: "I do think I am uniquely placed to take the heat off you. I'm here because I sniff out liars for a living."The faithful think I will identify the traitor by doing my job really well. If I'm on your side, I'll throw them off the scent."Taking the episode full circle, they each laid in a coffin, just as Winkleman had, to await their fate."I'm "90% that nice, warm guy who's on the news, but I'm also 10% psychopath," Rajan had said earlier.Although his Machiavellian side wasn't apparent when I sat opposite him for years at the BBC, it will be interesting to see what sort of a traitor he is - if he emerges from his coffin.

schema.headline: Celebrity Traitors: Chaos, coffins and ‘Claudiapatra’ steal the show

title: Why Gen Z are opting out of workplace pensions
description: 'It could cost me £10k but I need the money now': Why Gen Z are opting out of pensionsImage source, Hassan NassarImage caption, Dr Hassan Nassar is de
body: 'It could cost me £10k but I need the money now': Why Gen Z are opting out of pensionsImage source, Hassan NassarImage caption, Dr Hassan Nassar is determined to opt back in to his pension as soon as he canUntil early September, Hassan Nassar, 26, was saving around £430 every month into his NHS workplace pension.But the trainee GP, who works in the West Midlands, says he was "really cash strapped" and decided to stop putting money aside for around "six to 12 months".He needs the money to help take care of a sick family member, save for his first home and cover rent and student loan repayments.But he's aware there is a cost to opting out, estimating he could lose between "£5,000 and £10,000" in future retirement income due to the decades of compound interest he will miss out on by not saving now."People will say, you're silly, look at what you'll be missing out in the future," he tells the BBC. "But I need to look at what I'd be losing now if I didn't opt out."Future problemsAll employees will be automatically enrolled, external in a workplace pension if they are aged 22 or above and earn over £10,000, although there are exceptions.A percentage is taken directly from the worker's pay - usually around 5% - with tax relief added on top, and the employer must also pay a minimum contribution on top. But a growing number of Gen Z and millennials are opting out of these schemes due to cost-of-living pressures and the government has warned they could be on track for lower private pension incomes than people retiring today.That is a problem, because while most people in the UK will eventually get a state pension, it only provides a minimum level of retirement income and many will rely on a private pension to supplement it.Image source, Guido Mieth via Getty ImagesHassan says he was paying 10.7% of his gross earnings each month into his workplace pension, while the NHS contributed a substantial amount on top.But unlike some employers, the NHS doesn't allow staff to reduce their contributions when times are hard.  Overall, however, he is confident he will have enough to retire on at the end of his "30-40" year career and is determined to opt back in to his pension as soon as he can. According to the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), around 22.6 million people, or 90% of those who are eligible for "automatic enrolment" pensions, are paying into one, while about 2.5 million are not. However, Pensions Minister Torsten Bell told the BBC that "a rising number of young workers aren't saving, and overall there is a danger tomorrow's retirees are on track for lower private pension incomes than today's".According to DWP data, external: In the three months to December last year, 11.5% of eligible 22 to 29-year-olds who recently started a job opted out of their pensions. That's up from 6.6% in the same period of 2020. For 30 to 39-year-olds it's gone from 7.4% to 12.7%.'How can I save for a house?'Evie, 22, from Cornwall, says she opted out of entering the workplace pension at the London events company she works for.A recent drama school graduate, she says she would have struggled to cover her outgoings, including food, travel and the £800 she pays in rent. Evie is conscious about missing out on saving for retirement, but there are other things she needs money for that make it impractical right now. "How can I save for a house, how can I save for a car and afford my outgoings? I don't want to just work day in, day out to live, I want to work to have a life."'Think of your future self'April Leeson, from The Private Office, a chartered financial advice firm, says she would always advise people to not stop paying into their pensions if they can help it, even if that means reducing their contributions, which many employers allow you to do.This is partly because of the free employer contributions they will miss out on but also the lost compound interest."The current minimum pension age is 57, so any money you save in your 20s will have at least 30 years to compound and grow."£100 saved now, compounded at 4% a year over 30 years, is going to be worth a lot more than £100 saved in 15 to 20 years' time."She also urges younger people to think ahead. "You really need to think of your future self and what that person will need to retire comfortably."Kharlee, 47, a teacher from South East London, can certainly relate to this. She stopped her contributions to a workplace pension twice over the last five years for financial reasons. Image caption, Kharlee worries she won't have a comfortable retirementAnd she thinks she missed out on saving about £5,000 into her pension pot.She's in a better place financially now, but recently became self-employed and is no longer part of a private pension scheme, something she hopes to change."I would like to feel my pension is secure, and I don't feel like that. I worry I'm not going to be able to live comfortably at the age of retirement."Get in touchAre you able to save money every month? Share your tips with us on how you do it.

schema.headline: Why Gen Z are opting out of workplace pensions

title: Nations League: Craig Bellamy speaks out over abuse after Norway triumph
description: Former Wales striker Bellamy, who was appointed national boss in July 2024, faced criticism from some fans after holding talks over a potential move t
body: Former Wales striker Bellamy, who was appointed national boss in July 2024, faced criticism from some fans after holding talks over a potential move to Burnley in June.In a lengthy news conference after the Norway triumph, he said he feels people "could be kinder to each other" after revealing the negativity aimed at him had also affected his family."It's not me but I have kids and a wife; it's for them - they see it," he said."I've lived in this environment and I had it as a player, but I think there's ways we can speak to people, and just because it's the game we love, it doesn't give us the right to think we can say whatever we want to."We're such a small country, I'm like... why can't we have each other's backs? Why don't we look after each other more? Maybe that's me."I'm not saying everyone's above criticism, far from it. But I think it's too easy, and we're too quick."

schema.headline: Nations League: Craig Bellamy speaks out over abuse after Norway triumph

title: 2027 Cricket World Cup draw: England avoid Australia & India in group stage
description: England have avoided defending champions Australia and world number one-ranked side India in the group-stage draw for the 2027 ICC Men's Cricket World
body: England have avoided defending champions Australia and world number one-ranked side India in the group-stage draw for the 2027 ICC Men's Cricket World Cup.India and Pakistan are, once again, placed in the same group, alongside Australia, Afghanistan, Zimbabwe and a qualifier.England, who won the trophy in 2019, are in the same group as co-hosts South Africa, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, New Zealand and a qualifier.Harry Brook's side, who have enjoyed a resurgence in the 50-over format, begin their campaign against Bangladesh on 8 October, and Sri Lanka on 13 October in Windhoek, Namibia.They will come up against South Africa in Gqeberha on 16 October before travelling to Harare to face a qualifier on 20 October. They round off the group stage when they face New Zealand, again in Gqeberha, on 23 October.The visit to Zimbabwe is significant, with England having not played there since 2004.Political unrest in Zimbabwe under the regime of former president Robert Mugabe caused problems for England's men's team throughout the 2000s.England boycotted their fixture against Zimbabwe in Harare at the 2003 World Cup - a decision which ultimately derailed their campaign.Relations have improved in recent years, however, and BBC Sport reported in 2025 that the two cricket boards were discussing a potential England tour of the country in the next cycle of international cricket between 2027 and 2031.After three matches to decide the final two qualifiers, the tournament group stage will open with a repeat of the 2023 final when India and Australia face each other in Cape Town on 7 October.Arch-rivals India and Pakistan, who do not play each other outside tournaments, will meet in Johannesburg on 10 October.The top three, plus the best fourth-placed finisher, from the two groups progress to the Super 7 stage.From there, the top four teams will qualify for the semi-finals, which are scheduled for 17 and 18 November, before the final on 21 November in Johannesburg.

schema.headline: 2027 Cricket World Cup draw: England avoid Australia & India in group stage
